front: Name the three regions of an ultrasound beam.
back: Near field (Fresnel zone), focal zone (narrowest, best lateral resolution), and far field (Fraunhofer zone, beam diverges).

front: Where is lateral resolution best? Where is it worst?
back: Best at the focal zone. Worst in the far field where the beam widens.

front: Which is best: axial, lateral, or temporal resolution?
back: Axial resolution — determined by spatial pulse length. Improved by higher-frequency transducers (shorter wavelength).

front: Write-zoom vs read-zoom — which one improves resolution?
back: Write zoom (increases line density and pixels in the ROI). Read zoom just magnifies without adding resolution.

front: Describe reverberation artifact and give a common clinical example.
back: Multiple back-and-forth reflections between two strong parallel reflectors produce equally spaced, parallel lines of decreasing intensity beyond the object. Common with prosthetic valves.

front: How does a comet-tail artifact differ from a reverberation artifact?
back: Comet-tail also arises from a highly reflective (often metallic) object but appears as a solid hyperechoic beam distal to the object — lines are not equidistant. Both violate the time-of-flight assumption.

A structure placed in front of a highly reflective interface produces a duplicated copy at a deeper position (behind the reflector). The transducer misinterprets the multi-hop return path as a longer straight path.
Some ultrasound energy is emitted off the central beam axis; if it hits a strong reflector, the machine assumes it originated on-axis and displays the echo at the wrong lateral location.

front: What is a beam-width artifact and give an example.
back: When a structure at the edge of the beam is superimposed on the central image (occurs distal to the focal zone). E.g. aortic valve appearing 'in' the LA, or atheroma 'in' the aortic lumen. Adjust focal zone.

front: What law governs ultrasound refraction, and what causes it?
back: Snell's law. Refraction occurs when the beam crosses an interface obliquely between media with different propagation speeds — the beam bends, displacing structures laterally.

front: How do you fix a range-ambiguity artifact?
back: Increase the imaging depth. This lowers the PRF so echoes from the deepest structures return before the next pulse fires.

front: What is acoustic shadowing? Common source?
back: An anechoic (black) region distal to a strong reflector that attenuates the beam. Classic sources: mechanical prosthetic valves, calcifications, pacemaker wires.

front: Which artifacts appear at the SAME distance from the transducer as the true object?
back: Beam-width and side-lobe artifacts. Reverberation appears further than the object with parallel motion; mirror-image appears further with opposite motion.

front: Which imaging mode helps reduce side lobes, grating lobes, reverberation, and near-field clutter?
Mirror-image artifact in spectral Doppler — what causes it and how do you fix it?
back: Caused by excessive Doppler gain; a symmetric, lower-intensity signal appears on the opposite side of the baseline (crosstalk). Fix: decrease gain/power output, optimize angle.
Color signals extending beyond anatomic borders due to multiple reflections — often from moving structures or prosthetic material.

front: Explain propagation-speed-error artifact using the Starr-Edwards silastic ball.
back: US travels slower through the silastic ball than the assumed 1540 m/s, so distances appear longer than they are — the ball is displayed as oval rather than round.

front: How can you identify Type A vs Type B artifact around the ascending aorta on TEE?
back: Type A artifact: 2× as far from the transducer as from the posterior aortic wall (reverberation from the posterior aortic wall). Type B artifact: 2× distance from right PA posterior wall as from posterior aortic wall. Both move parallel to the aortic wall (no independent motion, unlike a true intimal flap).

front: How does frame rate change when you narrow the sector?
back: Frame rate increases (fewer scan lines per frame). Deeper depth, wider sector, and more focal zones all decrease frame rate.
